what_it_does: Quantum computers can only move information between certain pairs of physical quantum bits (called qubits) that are physically connected to each other; if two qubits that need to interact are not neighbors, the program must insert extra SWAP operations (swaps physically shuttle information across the chip). Tools that automatically figure out the best arrangement of a program onto a specific quantum chip — called quantum layout synthesis tools — are supposed to minimize these costly extra SWAP steps. The problem is that existing test circuits used to evaluate these tools happen to require zero SWAPs on the target chip, so the tools are never actually tested on the thing they are meant to optimize. This paper introduces QUBIKOS, a set of benchmark circuits where the minimum possible number of SWAPs is mathematically proven, giving tool developers an honest measuring stick. Running four leading tools against these benchmarks reveals they all fall well short of the proven minimum, exposing clear room for improvement.
